clinicalPearls: A disorder mainly of young children in which anagen hairs are poorly anchored and can be pulled out painlessly with little force
It typically presents in fair-haired girls aged around two to six with sparse, dull, unruly hair that seems never to need cutting and does not grow long
The hair-pull test easily extracts numerous anagen hairs, and light microscopy shows anagen roots lacking sheaths with a ruffled proximal cuticle and a distorted floppy-sock appearance
Trichoscopy may show rectangular black granular structures and solitary yellow dots
It is non-scarring with preserved follicular ostia, and hair anchorage tends to improve as the child grows
It is usually sporadic, though familial cases with autosomal dominant inheritance and associations with certain genetic syndromes are described
No specific treatment is required beyond gentle hair care and reassurance, as the condition generally improves spontaneously through childhood
reference.pathophysiology: Loose anagen syndrome results from defective anchorage of the hair shaft within the follicle owing to abnormal or premature keratinisation of the inner root sheath, so that cohesion between the shaft and the surrounding sheaths is impaired and anagen hairs are easily and painlessly extracted. Mutations affecting the companion-layer and inner-root-sheath keratin, including K6HF (KRT75), have been implicated. Because the follicles are structurally intact and not destroyed, the process is non-scarring and anchorage typically strengthens with maturity.
additionalDifferentials: Telogen effluvium, with club hairs, older patients and a trigger history
Alopecia areata, which is patchy with exclamation-mark hairs
Hair-shaft disorders causing fragility such as trichorrhexis nodosa
additionalInvestigations: Gentle hair-pull test extracting numerous anagen hairs
Light microscopy (trichogram) showing sheathless anagen roots with ruffled cuticles
Trichoscopy for solitary yellow dots and black granular structures
Assessment for associated ectodermal or syndromic features
Reassurance-based follow-up to document improvement with age
redFlags: Features suggesting an associated genetic syndrome such as dysmorphism or ectodermal defects
Progressive loss or scarring, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Onset or persistence into adulthood requiring exclusion of other causes
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and non-scarring, with hair anchorage and density generally improving spontaneously as the child grows, although hair may remain somewhat sparse or slow-growing.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting easily pulled hairs as alopecia areata or an effluvium
Overlooking associated syndromic features in familial cases
Subjecting children to unnecessary treatment for a self-limiting condition
Failing to perform trichogram microscopy, which is the key diagnostic test
management: Reassure families that this is a benign, non-scarring condition in which hair anchorage and density usually improve spontaneously as the child grows
Advise gentle hair care, avoiding traction, harsh brushing and chemical or heat treatments that dislodge the poorly anchored anagen hairs
Confirm the diagnosis with the hair-pull test and trichogram rather than pursuing unnecessary investigation, avoiding an erroneous label of alopecia areata
Consider topical minoxidil in persistent or cosmetically troublesome cases, recognising the evidence is limited
Assess for associated ectodermal or syndromic features and refer to clinical genetics if a broader syndrome is suspected
Provide dermatology follow-up to document improvement with age
